newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Rexrodt says yr 2000 jobs goal possible.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Rexrodt says yr 2000 jobs goal possible.

text.p: German economics minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday that Germany could still achieve the seemingly ever-more-difficult goal of halving its four million jobless total by the year 2000.
Rexrodt told German radio that the target, which Chancellor Helmut Kohl recently suggested might be too optimistic, could still be reached "under optimal conditions".
Among such conditions were that German wage negotiations show greater "flexibility" and that a major tax reform scheduled for 1999 was successfully implemented, he added.
Rexrodt also hinted that the government would be willing to discuss a second attempt of the so-called "Alliance for Jobs" initiative that failed earlier this year.

His comments follow a proposal made over the weekend by Germany's top trade union official for a "jobs summit" this year in which unions, politicians and employers would discuss ways to tackle unemployment, riding at a post-unification high.
The previous alliance, which earlier this year gained the support from trade unions, employers and the backing of the government itself, sought to link wage moderation to job creation measures.

But it failed when the unions accused Kohl's government of betrayal by pushing through a package of austerity measures which, among other things, was designed to cut a number of labour-related social costs.
Kohl sparked further anger among worker representatives in October when he suggested that a halving of German unemployment was perhaps too optimistic.

German unemployment in November rose 50,000 to a seasonally-adjusted 4.1 million, or 10.7 percent of the workforce, prompting some economic forecasters such as the respected RWI institute to suggest that Germany was stuck in an era of "jobless growth".

But recent 1997 wage accords in Germany's large metal and engineering and chemical industries, where pay rises of around inflation have been agreed, have been praised as not creating further obstacles to companies investing in labour.

Kohl's government, which faces an election in 1998, also believes that the 1999 tax reform would also contribute towards economic growth, and hence employment, by lowering the tax burden on consumers.

But Dieter Schulte, head of the DGB German Trade Union Federation, said on Sunday that summit talks on a complete restructuring of the labour market were necessary if the year 2000 two million jobless target was to be reached.
Schulte said on Sunday that a reduction in overtime hours and an increase in measures such as job-sharing were needed to bring the unemployment total down.
